name: Luna 9
short_status: Landed in Oceanus Procellarum 3 Feb 1966, transmitted until 6 Feb 1966; exact resting place still unconfirmed as of July 2026, with two rival candidate sites identified in early 2026.
tagline: Soviet Union · Lander · 1966 · The space race Success

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 31 January 1966, 11:41:37 UT (14:41:37 Moscow), Molniya-M (8K78M) from Site 31, Baikonur (Tyuratam)

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: 3 February 1966, 18:45:30 UT, Oceanus Procellarum west of Reiner and Marius craters, approx. 7.08 N, 64.37 W (official estimate)

facts.label: Landing capsule (ALS)
facts.value: 99 kg sealed sphere, 58 cm diameter, airbag-cushioned; ejected at about 5 m altitude and hit at 22 km/h, bouncing several times

facts.label: Full spacecraft
facts.value: 1,538 kg total at launch, 2.7 m tall (lander plus descent/cruise stage)

facts.label: Program context
facts.value: The USSR's 12th attempt at a lunar soft landing; chief designer Sergei Korolev died 14 January 1966, 17 days before launch

facts.label: Surface operations
facts.value: Petals opened about 4 minutes after touchdown; 7 radio sessions totaling 8 h 5 min and three series of TV pictures; first panorama transmission began 4 February at 01:50 UT

facts.label: Jodrell Bank interception
facts.value: Signals tracked from 16:29 UT on 3 February; pictures decoded 4 February 15:30-16:55 UT on a facsimile receiver borrowed from the Daily Express and published in Britain before the Soviet release

facts.label: 2026 site search
facts.value: npj Space Exploration paper (published 21 January 2026) flags a candidate object near 7.03 N, 64.33 W with confidence scores up to 77%; a separate crowdsourced candidate lies about 25 km away; both unconfirmed

timeline: Sergei Korolev, the chief designer behind the Luna program, dies during surgery in Moscow
Launch at 11:41 UT on a Molniya-M from Site 31 at Baikonur, the twelfth Soviet attempt at a lunar soft landing
16:29 UT: Jodrell Bank's Mark I telescope locks onto the descent signals
18:45:30 UT: The 99 kg capsule is ejected at about 5 m, hits at 22 km/h, bounces, and comes to rest in Oceanus Procellarum: the first survivable landing on another world
01:50 UT: First panorama transmission of the lunar surface begins
15:30 UT: Jodrell Bank prints the incoming pictures on borrowed Daily Express fax gear; British papers publish them before Moscow does
22:55 UT: Last contact after seven radio sessions totaling 8 h 5 min
NASA's Surveyor 1 achieves the first US soft landing, about four months after Luna 9
npj Space Exploration paper (Pinault et al., UCL) proposes a candidate lander near 7.03 N, 64.33 W using the YOLO-ETA machine-learning detector on LRO imagery
Mar 2026 (planned)
India's Chandrayaan-2 orbiter was slated to image both candidate sites at 0.25 m resolution; results not yet public (as of Jul 2026)
